title: The Ledger

narrative.text: The study smells of old wood and someone else's cigarettes. The previous Chancellor left in a hurry — there are still framed photographs on the wall, faces you don't recognize, men who ran this country for twenty-six years without asking permission. You have not taken them down yet. You're not sure why.
Vyktor Reznik arrives at 6:47 AM, exactly when he said he would. He carries a binder thick enough to stop a bullet. He does not congratulate you. He sets the binder on the desk and opens it.

Campaign intelligence understated the debt. Real figure is 340 million Krone. That is 16 percent of GDP. Interest payments alone consume 75 million a year. We're spending 65 million more than we take in.

Unemployment is 19 percent. Higher in Kravenstal and Sevagrad. Inflation is rising — 9 percent and accelerating. The Halvek regime cooked the books for the last three years. What was reported publicly was fiction.
I knew it was bad. Everyone knew it was bad. But there is a difference between knowing a number and sitting across from a man who reads it aloud with the affect of someone announcing the weather.

There's more. The military budget is overextended. Infrastructure maintenance has been deferred for 11 years. The BNI payroll alone is 20 million annually, for a service that officially doesn't exist. Can give you the full breakdown. Or can tell you what I think you need to hear first.
He waits. He is very good at waiting.

monologue: The previous Chancellor left photographs on the wall. Faces I don't recognize. I haven't taken them down yet. Not sure why. Vyktor reads the numbers with the affect of someone announcing the weather: 340 million in debt, 19 percent unemployment, a deficit of 65 million a year. I knew it was bad. Everyone knew. But there is a difference between knowing a number and sitting across from a man who reads it aloud while the previous Chancellor's photographs watch from the wall.

choices.text: "Give me everything. All of it. I need to understand the full shape of this before I make a single decision."

reactions.text: He turns the page. The motion is precise — a single page, but behind it are three hundred more. He begins reading aloud. He does not stop for three hours.

choices.text: "The deficit is the ceiling. Everything else is secondary until we have a plan to stop the bleeding. Walk me through the revenue options."

reactions.text: Revenue options. Three primary, two secondary. I will present by end of day.

He flips to a different tab in the binder — a section apparently already prepared for this exact question. He slides a single sheet across the desk. It is a list of every tax lever available to the government, ranked by political cost.

choices.text: "Give me a moment." You stand, move to the window. The city is still mostly dark. "Tell me what Halvek would have done in week one. I want to know what I'm inheriting before I decide what to burn."

reactions.text: He does not answer immediately. The question was not procedural. He is deciding whether the answer is safe to give.

Halvek would have called Oskar Brenner. Asked for a loyalty assessment of the general staff. Then cut the deficit by reducing the food subsidy. Then held a press conference praising the military. Three moves. Two of them are still viable.
